subject: Biology
title: Monarch Butterfly Migration
description: A micro-lesson that makes Monarch Butterfly Migration usable.

hook.text: No single monarch butterfly completes the full migration. It takes four generations to finish the loop.

buildup.text: Monarchs fly from Canada to central Mexico—up to 4,800 km—guided by the sun and magnetic fields.

discovery.text: The final generation enters a state called diapause—living 8 months instead of 5 weeks—to survive winter.

twist.text: No individual butterfly has made the trip before. The route information is encoded genetically.

climax.text: Habitat loss and herbicide-killed milkweed have cut monarch populations by over 80% in two decades.

punchline.text: A relay race across a continent, run by butterflies.

quiz.question: How many generations does it take to complete one monarch migration cycle?

details.summary: Monarch butterflies make a multigenerational migration spanning up to 4,800 kilometers between Canada and central Mexico. No single butterfly completes the round trip; it takes three to four generations to travel north, but a single super-generation flies the entire way south.
details.whyItMatters: The monarch migration is one of nature's greatest mysteries: how do butterflies navigate to a specific forest they have never visited? Their decline due to habitat loss makes understanding and protecting this phenomenon urgent.
takeaways: The southward super-generation lives up to eight months instead of weeks
Monarchs use a sun compass calibrated by a circadian clock for navigation
Milkweed loss in breeding grounds threatens the entire migration

faq.question: How do monarchs find the same wintering site they have never visited?
faq.answer: Monarchs use a time-compensated sun compass in their antennae combined with possible magnetic field sensing. The navigation program appears to be genetically encoded, directing them to specific oyamel fir forests in the mountains of Mexico.

faq.question: Why is the monarch migration declining?
faq.answer: Three main threats: milkweed loss from herbicide use in agricultural areas eliminates breeding habitat, deforestation in Mexican wintering sites removes critical shelter, and climate change disrupts the timing cues butterflies depend on.
